summary:
AstroHealth is a health-monitoring software demonstrator for long-duration space missions. It helps crew members record check-ins, review trends with timestamps, data sources, signal quality and missing readings, and find mission guidance when contact with Earth is delayed.
Its guided scenario uses synthetic exercise and recovery readings. It demonstrates a simulated sensor dropout, fictional check-in, communications interruption, local record queue and simulated receiver confirmation after reconnection. The local server remains available; spacecraft communications are not demonstrated.
The Mission Environment panel can query NASA DONKI events and show their UTC timestamps separately from crew data. These events do not indicate personal radiation dose. Crew readings are synthetic, not clinically validated, and not diagnostic.
Planned gamification would support routines and crew connection through flexible streaks, private progress, points for completed check-ins and optional team goals. Pauses carry no penalty, health rankings are excluded, and rest and medical guidance come first. Physical sensors, smart insoles, radiation instruments and secure mission integration remain future plans.
details:
AstroHealth is a web-based health-monitoring demonstrator for long-duration space missions. It helps crew members record self-reported check-ins and review synthetic health trends with timestamps, sources, signal quality, and missing readings. Its guided scenario shows exercise, sensor signal loss, a check-in, simulated communication loss, local data storage, recovery, and simulated receiver confirmation after reconnection. The local server remains available, and no physical sensors or spacecraft communication links are connected.

The Mission Environment panel queries NASA DONKI for timestamped space-weather events. These appear separately from crew readings and do not represent an individual’s radiation dose. The web prototype uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

AstroHealth’s creative approach combines data provenance, self-check-ins, and local record continuity in one crew-facing workflow. Planned gamification would encourage routines and crew connection through flexible goals, private progress, and optional team activities, without health rankings or penalties for rest. The project aims to support crew awareness and access to mission-approved guidance during communication delays. Its design considers data quality, privacy, accessibility, human review, and safety. It does not diagnose or provide clinically validated measurements.
